candidates.text: ​Portrait of a Place: Glacier View Once a year in Glacier View, Alaska, people drive enormous distances to watch their cars get catapulted off a 300ft cliff in one of the most scenic, remote parts of the world – an annual event known as the Fourth of July Car Launch. Drawing crowds from across the USA and beyond, the event stands as a depiction of unorthodox rituals, the American spirit, and catharsis, with many of the heavily decorated cars arriving with an attached emotional weight and personal history. Travelling to the event and spending time with its community, filmmaker Jamie Shipston-Mourn documents a human phenomenon of total destruction and spectacle in the name of celebration for the short film Glacier View . Finding the film through the people he met and their stories – among them, Ben Keefe, who spoke openly about addiction and sobriety – Shipston-Mourn captures a ceremony that is as much about the journey as the launch itself, presenting a chance for new beginnings by releasing regrets, memories and burdens in physical form against the majesty of the Alaskan landscape.

For a new short documentary, director Daniel Guix studies Delgado-Elias’ world through the house, exploring how our earliest encounters with spaces can mold our sensibility. Shooting on 16mm, to capture the grain, movement and texture of memory, Guix brings Delgado-Elias’ reflections into conversation with the house, as a rhythm that connects one room to the next, and a reminder of the formative impressions that unconsciously shape creative vision.

candidates.text: ​NOWNESS Shorts: Der Mann und sein Haus Constructing a celebration of stillness and the cinematic form, Indian-born filmmaker Kriti Dale explores the act of being present by stripping life to its essentials for the short film Der Mann und sein Haus – translated as The Man and His House . Through the life of 70-year-old Chi-Gong teacher Lambert in Uckermark, North Eastern Germany, the film presents a visual essay on self-sufficiency as both philosophy and daily practice, and the contentment found in mundane tasks. Against the endless skies and rusting birch trees of rural Brandenburg, Lambert chops wood, tends fire, cooks, and cleans the house built with his own hands, finding purpose in unadorned surroundings, and an appreciation of simplicity, quiet, and discipline. - Kriti Dale Working entirely in available light, with the camera held at a fixed distance, Dale shot on Kodak 500T 16mm film – overexposed and pull-processed to enhance the textures of solitude, from the rich blackness of night, to the soft highlights of open fire and daylight. Building the film around ambient sound – the hum of work and countryside, the call of the region’s native cranes, the crackle of the fire – Dale creates distance from the modern urban world beyond the frame, immersing viewers in a life of chosen stillness with just one lingering question: can a man truly be an island?
